NOTE: This is a very basic explanation of Brexit. As a result, it is not 100% accurate.

  • David Cameron, seeking to be reelected Prime Minister, needed votes from the Brexit fringe. He promises to provide a referendum (non-binding, of course) to determine whether the majority of the people within the UK would want the UK to remain or exit the EU.

  • Cameron keeps his word to allow the non-binding Brexit referendum, assuming that the voting majority would prefer the UK remain. Cameron realizes that more people want to leave the EU than he expected, so he campaigns for the UK to remain. Brexit proponents voted on the belief that the UK would no longer be obligated to the EU's rules (such as human rights and free travel [aka the refugees and Polish workers])

  • Guess what? The overall majority within the UK express their preference for the UK to exit the EU. However, the Brexit votes were territorial. Wales and England voted "leave," while Scotland, Northern Ireland, and Gibraltar voted "remain." All of the sudden, there is speculation of the UK being divided, with talk of Scottish independence and Irish reunification. Cameron, realizing he fucked up, resigns. People start to moan "boo hoo, I voted Leave, but I didn't expect Leave to win," realizing that their votes do count after all.

  • If a referendum shows an unprecedented preference to leave the EU, how does a nation leave the EU? A nation such as the UK would have to invoke Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty, the formal EU letter of resignation. There is no specified timetable for a country to invoke 50, but once the UK does so, it is permanent and there is no option of reversal, regardless of the aftermath, good or bad. However, the Brexit referendum is non-binding, and the UK's leaders, if they want to, can ignore the UK's majority voting to leave or stall Brexit as long as they can. As a result, the EU's exit provision turns out to be a Hobson's Choice, where, even though there is the exit option for EU members, the uncertainty of what would happen can deter them from following this procedure, even for the UK.

  • Theresa May, the UK's new Prime Minister, has said that the UK would not begin the Brexit procedure until 2018 at the earliest. However, officials representing May have confirmed that May can invoke 50 without a parliament vote. Whether or not she will really do so is still uncertain.
